CNN's Monday report, "Exclusive: US intel indicates Iran developing plans to
potentially detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, sources say," racked up
millions of views on social media. It wasn't the first existential threat
Americans have been handed of late.

The CNN article is paywalled, so most people never got to read the caveats:
that there's no intelligence to point to an imminent attack, that the Iranians
are thinking of planning to maybe do something, and that officials are arguing
over whether Tehran even has the ability to pull it off.

In other words, like Tucker Carlson's fever dream a few weeks ago that Trump
planned to nuke Iran, the dirty bomb story is a reminder that the mushroom
cloud sells. It also keeps the nuclear priesthood on top. (That's the weapons
labs, the Pentagon's nuclear planners and the arms-control experts whose
budgets and relevance depend on the bomb being the ultimate threat.)

How many times can we all be doomed? When the FAA grounds every flight and the
media compares it to 9/11 ad nauseam? When Microsoft goes down? When the chips
are flying away to China? When customers at Chase and other big banks can't
get into their accounts? On Tuesday it was Apple's turn. Then it was a
classified NSA network.

So many supposed calamities that it's almost funny. But it makes me wonder:
who benefits from these stories, and specifically who would want to leak the
Iran story?

A former senior intelligence official I talked to scoffed at CNN's dirty bomb
report, describing to me his own involvement in U.S. government contingency
planning more than a decade ago, a scenario he called "identical" to what CNN
reported.

He described a training exercise, overseen by the CIA, built around "an IRGC
plot to spirit a dirty bomb into the U.S." and staffed with Iranian,
Pakistani, and Afghan role players. The exercise, he recalled, came on the
heels of the Arab Spring and the Syrian chemical weapons crisis, which is what
appears to have prompted it.

In other words, the Iranian dirty bomb in Washington has been an imaginary
concern for over a decade and the subject of contingency planning for what to
do in response. The key word here is contingency: as in, dependent on
something else happening, no matter how unlikely. It's a government pastime.

Nuclear anything is a guarantee of front-page coverage and social media
virality, and it demands the White House's attention. "At this time there are
no credible threats to the homeland," Trump administration spokesperson Lauren
Bis told CNN, this from a White House not exactly known for underselling Iran.

In the case of the FAA outage, it is crystal clear who wins: the FAA. Though
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford says the agency is seeing "zero evidence of
anything nefarious," the Washington machine is already saying that a new
generation of equipment will have to be purchased for the poor, starved agency
and its antiquated equipment.

Then there's the need to spend more on cyber everything. Whether some weakness
or attack is the cause of any of the outages or not, the Washington machine is
ready with its ever-winning parable: This is why we need to spend more on
protecting the "critical" infrastructure. See what happens when just small
portions go down?

The threat machine (and its media lapdogs) is relentless.

Sen. Josh Hawley told TMZ, "You can't tell me it's a coincidence," in talking
about the various outages. Trump confidante Laura Loomer informed her
followers that the outages were what intelligence officials call "signaling,"
a "pre-warning before a major hack or debilitating cyber attack." A member of
Congress, demanding a briefing, simply referred to the FAA disaster as a
cyberattack, as though that had been established. Homeland Security Secretary
Markwayne Mullin went on Fox to float the idea that artificial intelligence
was moving too fast for older systems to keep up. People got so jumpy that
FEMA had to put out a statement reassuring the public that a routine, pre-
scheduled test of the Emergency Alert System was just that.

But then, the news media was blaring just a couple of weeks ago about the
Pentagon planning to build up 90 days of supplies if military bases go off-
grid. One would think that such news would provoke a spate of preppers buying
up everything, but then, why bother? Humanity is already doomed because of AI.

So, who leaked the dirty bomb story? And who leaked a similar story that
already ran in The New York Times that Iran had a secret arsenal of chemical
weapons?

The first and most likely culprit is the nuclear priesthood itself, needing to
reassert dominance over Iran policy now that the Democrats are taking power,
with the assumption that they will seek arms control and diplomacy to clean up
after Donald Trump.

Second is the Secret Service-DHS-FBI-cyber security-critical infrastructure
protection racket, guarding against the possibility of a reduction in national
security spending under the Democrats.

The third possibility is the Democrats themselves, who want it to be known
that despite Trump's war and all the bombing, Iran still presents a threat, a
grave one. But not so much a threat that more bombing is needed; hence WMD.
That makes the implications of continuing to fight a war too dangerous.

The fourth possibility is that the Trump White House leaked it, wanting to
change the narrative on the Iran war, that it was indeed necessary.

Fifth, the Israelis, who want it known not only that Iran is still a live
threat, but that the goal of regime change shouldn't be abandoned (look at how
crazy they are).

Sixth, it could be the intelligence agencies, always angling to meld with the
Hollywood image that they actually can see around the corner.

Seventh, it could be the Republicans, or conservatives in the administration,
or the pro-war set who want you to know that any letting up our guard is
fraught with danger, a counter to the second possibility. We can never spend
too much on war.

On social media, the people most skeptical of the CNN story and the motivated
leakers behind it are just repeating the Iraq WMD story. But then, their
postings only have any bounce because, like the earlier Tucker Carlson nuclear
story, they are talking about the end of the world.

2026 is coming to a close, and it was the year of the apocalypse. AI was going
to end us, or save us, depending on the week. So was the war. So were the
midterms. Every story arrived pre-inflated to the size of civilization itself.

In March, when all of Washington was bracing for a ground invasion of Iran, [I
reported](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/is-a-ground-war-with-iran-
imminent) that military sources told me it wasn't going to happen. CNN's
Michael Smerconish cited the story on air, introducing me as a guy who writes
"provocatively." That's where we are: declining to drink the Kool-Aid is the
provocative position.

The incentives for jacking up threats are real. I feel them. "Dirty bomb in
Washington" gets millions of views. "Contingency plan resembles 2012 training
exercise" does not. Fear is what people click on, and what people click on is
what pays the bills. It is hard to make a living telling readers that the
thing they're terrified of probably isn't going to happen.

I'm trying to anyway. Subscribe if you're sick of the fearmongering.
